info.title: Orebit Admin API
info.description:
Administrative backend for Orebit.

**No global prefix and no versioning.** Paths are literally `/auth/login`.

**Eight routes across four prefixes**, and the surface is kept small on purpose: the whole sign-in ceremony is one discriminated union on `POST /auth/login`, switched on `step`, and a route per step would mean nine places to get a guard right. `tests/app.routes.spec.ts` asserts the count.

**Errors** are RFC 9457 `application/problem+json`. Switch on `type` — a slug from the frozen catalogue in `src/contracts.ts` — never on the HTTP status, which is allowed to change.

**Success** is `{ "data": ... }`. Every `POST` returns 201.

### The ceremony

Three proofs, in order, none skippable:

1. `step: password` — argon2id + durable lockout + captcha. Returns `loginId` and emails a code. **No session.**
2. `step: verify-email` — advances to `EMAIL_VERIFIED`, answers `mfa_required` or `enrollment_required`. **No session.**
3. `POST /2fa` with `action: totp-verify` or `action: passkey-verify` — **the only place a session is minted.** These four factor actions MOVED off `/auth/login`; `LoginOutcome` has no `session` variant at all, so "this route cannot mint a session" is enforced by the type rather than by convention.

A seeded admin has no second factor, so their first sign-in enrolls one before any token exists.

`loginId` is the credential for every step past `password`, on this route and on `POST /2fa`. It is returned in the response body and sent back in the request body — there is no authentication cookie in the sign-in flow. Its server-side row carries the state, and `STEP_REQUIRES` in `auth/auth.types.ts` declares which states each step is legal from. A missing `loginId` is `validation_failed` (400), not `step_up_required`.

### Session transport

**The browser holds one secret: an opaque handle.** Neither token is ever returned in
a response body, and a browser never sends `Authorization`.

`POST /2fa {totp-verify | passkey-verify}` sets `orebit_admin_session` — httpOnly,
`Secure` in production, `SameSite=Lax`, `path=/`. Its value is a random 32-byte handle
naming a server-side record that holds the access token (15 min) and the refresh token.
Script on the page can read neither, so an XSS on the panel lifts a value that
authorises nothing off our origin.

**The token model behind that is unchanged.** The access JWT is still what authenticates
a request, still verified the same way, and the session row is still checked on every
call — so a logout or a detected refresh replay takes effect immediately rather than at
the end of a token's fifteen minutes. What moved is only where the tokens are kept.

**Refresh is automatic and invisible.** When the stored access token nears expiry the
backend rotates the pair itself, mid-request, under a per-session lock. The handle in
the cookie does not change, so a client sees nothing. There is no refresh endpoint;
`POST /auth/session {action: 'refresh'}` was removed.

**CSRF applies to every mutating request**, because a root-scoped cookie means the
browser attaches the credential without the page asking. Read `csrfToken` from the
session response (or the readable `orebit_admin_csrf` cookie) and send it back in the
`x-csrf-token` header on every POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE. The token is
`nonce.HMAC(pepper, nonce:handle)`, not a bare random value — plain double-submit is
defeated by a sibling subdomain, which can WRITE a cookie on the parent domain without
being able to read one.

### Establishing and ending a session

`GET /auth/session` answers "am I signed in, and until when". A standalone frontend
cannot inspect an httpOnly cookie, so it needs this once on load and again whenever the
session may have changed elsewhere — returning to a tab, reconnecting. It carries
`Cache-Control: no-store` and does NOT count as activity, so polling it cannot hold an
abandoned session open.

A 401 carries the reason as its `type`: `session_revoked` (ended elsewhere),
`token_expired` (timed out), `unauthenticated` (no usable cookie). Treat 403 as
"this action is not permitted" and do **not** sign the admin out for it.

`POST /auth/session {logout | logout-all}` revokes server-side, deletes the stored
record, and expires both cookies. Idempotent — repeating it succeeds.

**Two clocks bound a session**, and they are not interchangeable. `refreshExpiresAt` is
the idle deadline: the current implementation uses a **30-minute idle window with five-minute write throttling** (`AdminSession.lastActiveAt` advances on eligible requests at most once every five minutes).
It is deliberately NOT moved by the backend's own token refresh, nor by
`GET /auth/session`, which is a poll. `reauthenticateAt` is the absolute ceiling from
the original three-factor sign-in (12 hours); nothing extends it, so it is the value to count down
to when warning that a full sign-in is coming.

An idle-expired session answers 401 `token_expired` (with `message.code` `SESSION_EXPIRED` on `GET /auth/session`), distinct from `session_revoked`.

### Per-action re-authentication

Every mutating request carries a single-use ticket in `x-elevation-ticket`, obtained from `POST /2fa {action: 'reauth-verify', intent: '<the write>'}`. The ticket is bound to the session that minted it AND to the named action, and is consumed by one spend — so one proof buys one specific write, not sixty seconds of unrestricted access.

tags.name: auth
tags.description: sign-in ceremony, sessions, recovery, current admin

tags.name: 2fa
tags.description: Second-factor management for an admin who is already signed in. Authorised by a bearer access token, plus a password re-check on every change to the factor set. Distinct from the MFA steps of POST /auth/login, which are gated by `loginId`.

tags.name: admins
tags.description: Super-admin actions on other administrators: factor recovery, disable, enable.

tags.name: kyc
tags.description:
Configuring identity verification, and granting relief from it.

This service WRITES `identity.kyc_policies`, `identity.kyc_policy_versions` and `identity.kyc_exemptions`. It does not enforce them: the user backend reads those tables directly out of the shared database and applies them. There is no API between the two services, so a write here reaches enforcement as soon as it commits.

What this surface deliberately cannot touch: what an account has actually PROVED. Verifications, profiles and provider events belong to the user backend and arrive over a signed webhook from the provider. No route here can manufacture one.

tags.name: countries
tags.description:
Two surfaces that must not be confused.

**`/countries/images` is the IMAGE LIBRARY** — objects in the Cloudflare R2 bucket. List them, or add one. An asset here may be used by many countries or by none, and uploading one creates NO country record.

**`/countries` is the CATALOGUE** — rows in `admin.countries`, each holding the two object keys an admin chose.

The flow is: browse or upload → get object keys → `POST /countries` with those keys. A country is therefore created complete, with both flags already chosen.

Uploads land at `country-assets/{ISO}/{type}/{uuid}.webp`, so a new image NEVER overwrites one an existing country still points at. The client always passes an object **key**, never a URL: a key cannot express another origin, and one is refused unless it parses as ours, sits in the claimed slot, and names an object that really exists.

SUPER_ADMIN only. No path parameters anywhere — the ISO code travels in a body field, a multipart field, or the query string.

tags.name: chat
tags.description: Chat administration: rooms, rules, moderation, staff, skins, media and chat-wide settings.

get.description: Is this process alive. Touches no dependency, deliberately — a load balancer that kills the process because Postgres blinked turns one outage into two.
Can this process serve traffic. Checks Postgres and Redis; this is the one a deploy gate should read.

post.summary: The sign-in ceremony — all nine steps
post.description:
The FIRST HALF of the sign-in ceremony: password, emailed code, and the state read that lets a refreshed page resume. It ends at EMAIL_VERIFIED and mints no session.

The second factor is proven on POST /2fa, which is the only place a session is issued. The same `loginId` carries the caller across. An outcome of `mfa_required` or `enrollment_required` means 'continue at /2fa'.

state.summary: where am I (resume after a refresh)

201.description: The step's outcome. Only `outcome: "session"` carries tokens.

post.description:
Guarded by `OptionalAuthGuard`, so a repeated logout succeeds and an admin whose session expired while they were away is still signed out cleanly rather than getting a 401.

Revokes the session family server-side, deletes the stored token record, and expires both cookies. `logout` ends this sign-in; `logout-all` ends every session for the account.

The `refresh` action was removed — see the request schema.

logout.description: Send the `orebit_admin_session` cookie and the matching `x-csrf-token` header.

logoutAll.summary: End every session for this account

201.description: `{ message: { code: "LOGGED_OUT", text } }`. Both cookies are expired with `Max-Age=0`. Idempotent — repeating it succeeds with the same body.

Set-Cookie.description: On `logout` and `logout-all`: both cookies (`orebit_admin_session` and `orebit_admin_csrf`) are cleared with `Max-Age=0`.

503.description:
`session_store_unavailable`. The session store could not be reached, so the server could not identify which session to revoke and did NOT perform a revocation. Nothing was logged out. The session cookie is deliberately LEFT IN PLACE so the client still holds the handle needed to retry — clearing it would strand a live session that could never be revoked. Retry once the dependency recovers.

Distinct from a 201: a store that answers "no such session" is an ordinary success, because there is nothing left to revoke.

get.summary: Is this browser signed in, and as what
get.description:
The one call a standalone frontend needs on load. It cannot inspect an httpOnly cookie, so it cannot tell from the cookie alone whether it is signed in — this answers that.

Returns `{ role, permissions, authenticated, lastActiveAt, message }`. `permissions` is always empty for now.

A 200 means the session is live. A 401 carries the REASON as its `type` slug (`session_revoked`, `token_expired`, `unauthenticated`) with `extra` describing the signed-out state (`message.code`). There is no `authenticated: false` 200 response.

Does NOT count as activity. Polling this — on tab focus, on reconnect, on a timer — must not extend the idle deadline, or an abandoned tab would hold a session open indefinitely by asking whether it was still open.

Responses are `Cache-Control: no-store`. Do not cache them.

401.description: Login required. Branch on `type`: `session_revoked` (ended elsewhere), `session_expired` (idle timeout), or `unauthenticated` (no usable cookie). All three call for the same cleanup; only `session_revoked` is an event someone else caused.

get.description: Read from the database rather than reconstructed from the token's claims — an access token lives fifteen minutes, so its `rol` may be stale, and this is what a UI uses to decide what to show.

200.description: The authenticated admin, their session id, and the CSRF token to mutate with.

csrfToken.description: The value to echo in the `x-csrf-token` header on every mutating request — the same token `POST /auth/login` returns on completion, reported again here so it survives a reload. A panel served from a different origin than this API cannot read the `orebit_admin_csrf` cookie, so this is the only way it can relearn the token. Reading it does not rotate it: an existing valid token is returned unchanged. Null when the request authenticated with a bearer token, which is never asked for a CSRF token.

get.description: Everything the CALLING admin can sign in with. Confirmed factors only — a pending TOTP enrollment is a QR code nobody proved they scanned. There is no adminId parameter anywhere in this module, so one admin cannot read another's factors.

post.summary: Add, confirm, rename or remove a second factor
post.description:
EVERY second-factor action, as one discriminated union on `action`.

## Three credential groups
1. **Sign-in** (`totp-enroll`, `totp-verify`, `passkey-challenge`, `passkey-verify`) — the `loginId` from POST /auth/login, at state EMAIL_VERIFIED. No access token exists yet. These mint the session.
2. **Re-auth** (`reauth-challenge`, `reauth-verify`) — a bearer token. Proving a factor yields a SINGLE-USE elevation ticket, valid ~60s.
3. **Management** (`totp-add`, `passkey-add-challenge`, `rename`, `remove`) — a bearer token AND a ticket in `X-Elevation-Ticket`. One proof, one write.

`totp-confirm` and `passkey-add-verify` need no ticket: each is the second half of a flow whose first half already spent one, and each is gated by a pending row or a single-use challenge.

There is no password field anywhere — re-proving a second factor replaced it.

**Passkeys are the intended factor for re-auth.** A TOTP step can be claimed exactly once, so codes cap at one write per 30 seconds; TOTP is accepted by `reauth-verify` only so an admin without a passkey can reach `passkey-add-challenge`.

201.description: The action's outcome. Only `session` carries tokens; only `totp_enrollment` carries a secret; `elevated` carries a ticket.

403.description: reauth_required — no live elevation ticket for this write.

404.description: No such factor on this account.

409.description: mfa_not_enrolled, mfa_already_enrolled, totp_replayed, passkey_already_registered, or step_up_step_invalid.

parameters.name: X-Elevation-Ticket
parameters.description: Single-use ticket from reauth-verify. Required by every action that changes the factor set.

post.description:
SUPER_ADMIN only, and the ONLY route in this service whose actions target an account other than the caller's own. Every action needs a bearer access token AND a fresh elevation ticket in `x-elevation-ticket`, proved for that action's own name (see `intent` on POST /2fa reauth-verify).

The role is checked against a freshly-read database row, not the token's `rol` claim: an access token lives 15 minutes, so a demoted admin must not keep this reach until it expires.

Every action revokes the target's sessions and emails the target. An administrative action that could be taken silently is one a compromised admin session could take silently.

resetFactors.summary: Recover an admin who lost their authenticator
resetFactors.description:
Empties the target's second-factor set so their next sign-in enrols a new one, exactly as a freshly seeded account does. Requires an elevation ticket proved for `admin.factors.reset`.

This is NOT delivered by email, and that is the point: email is already the second factor, so an emailed factor reset would make the mailbox sufficient on its own.

value.reason: lost their phone, verified by video call

disable.summary: Take an account out of service

resolveLoginReview.summary: Decide a suspension opened by repeated lockouts
resolveLoginReview.description: The human half of the lockout ladder. Read the queue first to get `expectedVersion`; a stale one is refused rather than silently overwriting another reviewer's decision.

value.reason: Confirmed with the account owner by phone; locked out by a typo.

400.description: validation_failed — including an action that may not target your own account.

401.description: unauthenticated — no session, or the caller's own account is disabled or deleted.

403.description: forbidden (not a SUPER_ADMIN) or reauth_required (no live elevation ticket for this action).

get.summary: The accounts a repeated lockout has suspended
get.description:
SUPER_ADMIN only. Lists accounts the lockout ladder has taken out of service, each with a summary of the authentication events that put it there.

An account reaches this queue by being locked twice inside the 30-day strike memory: ten consecutive wrong passwords earns a one-hour lock, and ten more while that strike is still remembered suspends the account entirely. No wait restores it — a super admin decides, through POST /admins {action:"resolve-login-review"}.

Unlike every other route on this prefix this one takes NO elevation ticket: it reads and changes nothing, so the gate is a full session plus the SUPER_ADMIN check, which is the same bar GET /2fa sets. The role is read from a freshly loaded database row rather than the token's `rol` claim.

parameters.name: status
parameters.description: Defaults to PENDING — "what needs my attention" is the overwhelmingly common read. RESOLVED and REJECTED answer "what did we decide last time".

401.description: No session, or the caller's own account is not active.

403.description: The caller is not a SUPER_ADMIN.

get.description:
SUPER_ADMIN only. Returns the policies that EXIST, plus the vocabularies a form needs.

Unlike the security-restriction surface, this cannot enumerate its whole target space — that is every ISO country times two levels — so an un-created policy has no placeholder row. `createVersion` states what to send as `expectedVersion` to create one.

`enforcementRejection` is null for a policy the user backend will act on. A non-null value means that service would silently DISCARD the row, so the policy is configured and enforcing nothing. Every value this API can write passes, so a non-null result means the database constraints and the consumer's rules have diverged.

401.description:
No usable access token, or the session is revoked.

Error `type` values: `unauthenticated`, `token_invalid`, `session_revoked`

403.description:
The caller is authenticated but is not a super admin, or the write carried no valid elevation ticket.

The role is re-read from the database rather than taken from the token, so a demoted admin loses this reach immediately rather than when the token expires.

Error `type` values: `forbidden`, `reauth_required`

post.summary: Create, update or remove a KYC policy
post.description:
SUPER_ADMIN only, plus a fresh elevation ticket in `x-elevation-ticket`. The ticket is proved for the action NAMED IN THE BODY — `admin.kyc-policy.update` or `admin.kyc-policy.delete` — so a proof bought for editing a policy cannot remove one.

**Compare-and-swap.** Send `expectedVersion: 0` to create, or the version you read to update. If the row has moved since, the write is refused with `400 validation_failed` on `expectedVersion` and the current version is named — re-read and re-present rather than retrying.

**Disabling is not removing.** The user backend resolves an exact country policy before the global `*` one, and a DISABLED country policy STILL WINS its region. Setting `enabled: false` therefore means “this region has a rule and it is off”; it does not restore the global rule. `action: "delete"` is the only thing that does, and it appends a tombstone version so the history stays complete.

**Every field is written.** There is no partial update: omitting a nullable field is a validation error rather than a silent clear, so a half-filled form cannot wipe a live threshold.

201.description: The policy was written. Returns the whole table.

400.description:
The body is invalid, or the compare-and-swap lost.

Validation mirrors every CHECK constraint on the table, so a refusal here is a refusal the database would also have made — plus three rules it cannot express: an enabled `triggersOnly` policy with nothing to trigger on (which would make verification permanently unreachable in that region), a threshold currency with no threshold, and renewal settings with renewal off.

Error `type` values: `validation_failed`

401.description:
No usable access token, or the session is revoked.

Error `type` values: `unauthenticated`, `token_invalid`, `session_revoked`

403.description:
The caller is authenticated but is not a super admin, or the write carried no valid elevation ticket.

The role is re-read from the database rather than taken from the token, so a demoted admin loses this reach immediately rather than when the token expires.

Error `type` values: `forbidden`, `reauth_required`

get.summary: The version history for one policy target
get.description:
SUPER_ADMIN only. Every recorded version of the policy for one `(region, level)`, newest first, so an operator can answer who changed it, when, what it said and what it replaced.

Append-only: there is no route that edits or deletes a version, and the service has no method that could. A removal appends a tombstone rather than erasing the history.

parameters.name: region
parameters.description: `*` for the global policy, or an ISO-3166-1 alpha-2 country.

400.description:
The query is missing a target or carries an out-of-range limit.

Error `type` values: `validation_failed`

401.description:
No usable access token, or the session is revoked.

Error `type` values: `unauthenticated`, `token_invalid`, `session_revoked`

403.description:
The caller is authenticated but is not a super admin, or the write carried no valid elevation ticket.

The role is re-read from the database rather than taken from the token, so a demoted admin loses this reach immediately rather than when the token expires.

Error `type` values: `forbidden`, `reauth_required`

get.description:
SUPER_ADMIN only. With `userId`, one account's full history. Without it, every account that currently holds relief — the compliance-review question, and bounded, because at most one live exemption exists per account.

`live` is computed by the DATABASE, not by this service: the user backend decides whether an exemption applies using the database clock, and an admin screen using its own could disagree with the service actually gating the user.

parameters.name: userId
parameters.description: Omit to list everyone currently exempt.

400.description:
The query is malformed.

Error `type` values: `validation_failed`

401.description:
No usable access token, or the session is revoked.

Error `type` values: `unauthenticated`, `token_invalid`, `session_revoked`

403.description:
The caller is authenticated but is not a super admin, or the write carried no valid elevation ticket.

The role is re-read from the database rather than taken from the token, so a demoted admin loses this reach immediately rather than when the token expires.

Error `type` values: `forbidden`, `reauth_required`

post.summary: Grant or revoke a KYC exemption
post.description:
SUPER_ADMIN only, plus a fresh elevation ticket proved for `admin.kyc-exemption.grant` or `admin.kyc-exemption.revoke` — separate actions, so a proof for one cannot spend the other.

**This is the most consequential write in the service.** The user backend folds a live exemption into an account's EFFECTIVE verification level on every evaluation, so a grant raises that account's standing platform-wide the moment it commits, with no provider attesting anything. It does not write a verification and does not move the account's verified level, so “verified” and “exempted” stay separable in every export.

**One live exemption per account.** Granting to an account that already holds one is refused with `409`; revoke it first, so the record shows which grant was in force when. An account whose exemption merely LAPSED is not refused — the lapsed row is closed automatically, because it would otherwise occupy the account's only slot while granting nothing.

**There is no edit.** Changing an exemption is a revoke followed by a grant, so both facts stay on the record.

`expiresAt` is required and nullable: `null` is a permanent exemption, and it has to be typed out rather than defaulted into.

201.description: The exemption was granted or revoked.

400.description:
The body is invalid, or the exemption named was already revoked.

Error `type` values: `validation_failed`

401.description:
No usable access token, or the session is revoked.

Error `type` values: `unauthenticated`, `token_invalid`, `session_revoked`

403.description:
The caller is authenticated but is not a super admin, or the write carried no valid elevation ticket.

The role is re-read from the database rather than taken from the token, so a demoted admin loses this reach immediately rather than when the token expires.

Error `type` values: `forbidden`, `reauth_required`

404.description:
No such account, or no such exemption for that account. An exemption belonging to a DIFFERENT account answers 404 as well — confirming it exists would make this route an oracle for enumerating exemption ids.

Error `type` values: `not_found`

409.description:
The account already holds a live exemption. Revoke it before granting a replacement.

Error `type` values: `kyc_exemption_active`

get.description:
Super-admin. X and Y, the two GLOBAL periods that decide when a completed verification goes stale. Not per country and not per level — a single row, and a route shape that cannot express a narrower one.

Both ship NULL, which means nothing ever expires and same-level redo stays closed. That is a configuration, not an absence: no default is ever substituted.

A pure read. It writes nothing and records no audit event.

404.description: The singleton row is missing — a deployment fault, since the consumer migration seeds it.

post.description:
Super-admin. Full-state write of the two periods onto the one settings row.

⚠ The first non-null `mandatoryPeriodDays` invalidates every account whose verification predates it, simultaneously and with no grace period, and writing the old value back does not undo it — only the holders re-verifying does.

Both fields are required: a field sent as null turns that half of renewal OFF, so omitting one cannot mean "leave it alone". Sending both as null disables renewal entirely.

Days in, whole seconds stored. There is no `expectedVersion`, no `reason` and no configuration history — who changed the periods is recorded as `ADMIN_KYC_RENEWAL_SETTINGS_UPDATED` in the admin audit log.

201.description: Written. The response is the stored configuration, re-read.

400.description:
Y at or above X, Y without X, a non-positive or fractional period, a period over 36500 days, a missing field, or an unknown field such as `expectedVersion`, `reason` or `renewalEnabled`.

Error `type` values: `validation_failed`

get.description:
Super-admin, **read-only**. The permanent record of every KYC attempt any account has ever made — started, failed, abandoned, expired and approved, including the successes a later renewal replaced. Nothing is ever deleted and no newer attempt overwrites an older one.

This surface has no write handler and cannot approve a case, move a verification through its state machine, start a session, or touch a level state. A decision belongs to the provider and arrives over a signed webhook.

**It is observational: querying it never triggers renewal**, whatever the global periods are set to — including the shipped state where both are null and renewal is off.

Newest first, ordered (createdAt DESC, id DESC). Page with `cursor` — keyset rather than offset, because history only grows and an offset would repeat or skip rows as attempts land underneath a paging operator. Every read is audited.

parameters.name: from
parameters.description: Lower bound on when the attempt STARTED.

parameters.name: cursor
parameters.description: Opaque. Send back the nextCursor from the previous page; anything else is refused.

400.description:
A malformed uuid, an unknown level or status, a backwards date range, a tampered cursor, or an unknown parameter.

Error `type` values: `validation_failed`

get.description:
Super-admin, **read-only**. One attempt with the devices the provider observed during it and the deliveries that settled it.

The verification is targeted by query parameter rather than a path segment: this service takes no path parameters anywhere, so that the answer to which accounts a route can reach stays in one validated place.

Provider events are correlated by the attempt own sessionId. Their verified bodies are never returned.

200.description: The attempt, its devices and its provider deliveries.

400.description:
A missing or malformed verificationId.

Error `type` values: `validation_failed`

get.summary: The catalogue — countries that exist, with their flag URLs
get.description:
SUPER_ADMIN only. Reads `admin.countries` and **never the bucket**. Without `isoCode`, every country; with it, that one.

A country appears here only once it has been created — uploading an image does not do that. For the flags available to choose from, use `GET /countries/images`, which is a different question and a different answer.

Every row carries `name` and `isoCode` beside both URLs, so a client never has to infer which country an image belongs to. At most 249 rows, so there is no pagination.

parameters.name: isoCode
parameters.description: Omit to list every country. Case-insensitive.

400.description:
The query is malformed, or the ISO code is not an assigned one.

Error `type` values: `validation_failed`

401.description:
No credential, or the session is gone.

Error `type` values: `unauthenticated`

403.description:
Not a super admin.

Error `type` values: `forbidden`

404.description:
A valid ISO code with no country configured. Reported rather than an empty list: the caller named a specific country.

Error `type` values: `not_found`

post.summary: Create a country from two chosen images
post.description:
SUPER_ADMIN only. The last step of the flow: the admin has already picked or uploaded both flags, and this turns them into a catalogue row.

Each key is validated twice before anything is inserted:

1. **Is it ours, and in the right slot?** The key must parse as one of our two layouts and its own slot must match the field it was sent in. A URL cannot parse at all.
2. **Does the object exist?** A HEAD against the bucket, so a well-formed key for an object nobody uploaded is refused rather than stored as a permanent 404.

A missing asset is reported as a validation failure on the offending FIELD, so a UI can put the error next to the picker that produced it. A storage outage is **503** instead — "we could not ask" must never be reported as "your image is missing".

201.description: The country, with both image URLs.

400.description:
The body is malformed; the name or code is invalid; an image key is not one of ours, is in the wrong slot, or names an object that does not exist; or an unknown property such as `roundImageUrl` was sent.

Error `type` values: `validation_failed`

401.description:
No credential, or the session is gone.

Error `type` values: `unauthenticated`

403.description:
Not a super admin.

Error `type` values: `forbidden`

409.description:
A country with this ISO code already exists. Nothing was malformed, so this is not a 400.

Error `type` values: `country_already_exists`

503.description:
The bucket could not be reached to confirm the images exist. Nothing was written.

Error `type` values: `country_image_storage_unavailable`

get.summary: The image library — flags available to choose from
get.description:
SUPER_ADMIN only. Every country image in the R2 bucket, newest first.

This is what the Create Country screen calls so an admin can pick an existing flag instead of uploading one. It reads **object storage only** and never the country table, which is what makes selection possible for a country that does not exist yet.

Both key layouts are listed: the current `country-assets/{ISO}/{type}/{uuid}.webp` and the original `countries/{ISO}/{type}.webp`. An object whose key does not parse is skipped rather than guessed at — the bucket may hold things this service did not write, and inventing a type for one would put a mystery object in a flag picker.

An unreachable bucket is **503**, never an empty list: showing an empty library when the truth is "we could not ask" would invite an admin to re-upload flags that exist.

parameters.description: Show only assets filed under this code. Case-insensitive.

parameters.name: type
parameters.description: Show only round or only square assets — a round picker has no use for square ones.

200.description: The available assets. An empty list means an empty bucket.

400.description:
The query is malformed, or `type` is not round/square.

Error `type` values: `validation_failed`

No credential, or the session is gone.

Error `type` values: `unauthenticated`

Not a super admin.

Error `type` values: `forbidden`

post.summary: Add ONE image to the library
post.description:
SUPER_ADMIN only. `multipart/form-data` with one file plus `isoCode` and `type`.

**Creates no country and requires none to exist.** It puts an object in the bucket and returns its key and public URL; the client renders the URL as a preview and sends the key to `POST /countries` afterwards. An upload never followed by a create simply leaves an asset in the library for the next admin — that is the feature working, not a leak, which is why there is no cleanup worker.

One image per request: an admin may replace only the round flag and keep the square one they already had.

Every upload mints a NEW key, so it can never overwrite an image an existing country points at.

Content is decoded to determine its format — the filename and the part's `Content-Type` are never trusted. Must be square, at most 512x512 and at most 1 MiB. Animated images and SVG are refused. Everything is re-encoded to metadata-free lossless WebP, which strips EXIF/GPS and is why a stored key always ends `.webp`.

isoCode.description: Where the asset is FILED. Not a country that must exist. May be sent before or after the file.

type.description: Declared by the caller: a round flag and a square one are both square rasters, so nothing in the bytes says which frame it is for.

201.description: The stored asset. Use `key` in POST /countries and `url` for a preview.

400.description:
A field is missing or invalid, the file field is not named `image`, or the image is not a format this service stores.

Error `type` values: `validation_failed`, `country_image_invalid`

401.description:
No credential, or the session is gone.

Error `type` values: `unauthenticated`

403.description:
Not a super admin.

Error `type` values: `forbidden`

413.description:
The image exceeded 1 MiB, before or after normalisation.

Error `type` values: `country_image_too_large`

503.description:
Object storage could not be reached, or is unconfigured. Nothing was written.

Error `type` values: `country_image_storage_unavailable`

bearerAuth.description: The ES256 access token. Its `aud` is pinned to `orebit-admin/access`, so a refresh token presented here is rejected inside `jwt.verify`.

cookieAuth.name: orebit_admin_session
cookieAuth.description:
The browser's credential: an opaque 32-byte handle naming a server-side record that holds the access and refresh tokens. httpOnly, Secure in production, SameSite=Lax, path `/`. Script cannot read it, and it means nothing to anyone who cannot reach our Redis.

Every mutating request must also carry `x-csrf-token`, echoing the readable `orebit_admin_csrf` cookie — see `Session.csrfToken`.

Retry-After.description: Present only when the problem body carries `retryAfterSeconds`, and always the same number. Listed in `Access-Control-Expose-Headers`, so browser JavaScript on the admin panel origin can read it; the body field needs no such arrangement and is the simpler thing to parse.

type.description: The error slug. THE thing a client switches on.

extra.description: Machine-readable extras — e.g. `attemptsRemaining` on a wrong code, `state` on a wrong step.

retryAfterSeconds.description: Seconds until a retry is allowed. Optional, and today only two slugs carry it: `account_locked` (3600 on the first lockout, then the time remaining on it) and `rate_limited` (the window's remaining TTL, or the captcha penalty's). OMITTED ENTIRELY — never `0`, never `null` — when no wait applies. `admin_login_manual_review` and `account_disabled` are the refusals that matter here: nothing but a super admin's decision lifts either, so a countdown rendered against one would expire into another refusal. Absence of this field is therefore the statement "there is nothing to wait for", and must be read as such rather than as a missing value. The same number is also sent as the `Retry-After` response header, exposed to the admin panel via `Access-Control-Expose-Headers`; read either, and prefer this field.

Session.description: A minted session. NOTE there are deliberately NO TOKEN FIELDS. Both the access token and the refresh token are held server-side, in the record named by the opaque `orebit_admin_session` httpOnly cookie (path `/`, SameSite=Lax, Secure in production). The browser presents that cookie and nothing else; it never sends an `Authorization` header, and script on the page can read neither token. The backend rotates the pair itself, mid-request, when the access token nears expiry — so there is no refresh call for a client to make.

refreshExpiresAt.description: The IDLE deadline: when the session dies if it is not used. Moves forward on ACTIVITY — a real request — and deliberately not on token refresh, which the backend does on its own schedule. The name predates the cookie change and is kept so the contract does not break.

reauthenticateAt.description: The ABSOLUTE ceiling from this sign-in, fixed for the life of the session. Nothing extends it. This is the value to count down to when warning an admin that a full three-factor sign-in is coming; `refreshExpiresAt` keeps moving while they work and so can never warn.

csrfToken.description: Echo this in the `x-csrf-token` header on EVERY mutating request (POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE). Also set in the readable `orebit_admin_csrf` cookie; this field is here for clients that cannot read cookies. Required because the session cookie is root-scoped, so every such request is cookie-authenticated: the browser attaches the credential without the page asking, and a token the attacker's page cannot read is what distinguishes a real request from a forged one. Not a credential — it authorises nothing on its own.

Bearer. Send EXACTLY ONE of response (passkey) or code (TOTP). Yields a single-use elevation ticket, BOUND TO ONE ACTION — see `intent`.

intent.description: WHICH write this proof is for, e.g. `rename` or `admin.factors.reset`. The ticket is bound to it and the route that spends it names the same value independently, so a proof given for one action is refused by another — without this, one tap authorises any mutating route for 60 seconds, which is a time window rather than a per-action proof. Omitting it binds the ticket to a wildcard accepted ONLY by the twelve factor actions on POST /2fa, never by /admins or any future mutating route. Optional for now for backwards compatibility; treat it as required.

May NOT target your own account: the whole point of a review is to put a human other than the account holder between a repeatedly-locked account and being signable-into again, so resolving your own would be the review not happening.

decision.description:
ENABLE restores the account and clears its lockout state, INCLUDING the strike memory — this is the only thing in the service that clears it, because a human deciding "this was our own admin fumbling" is the only evidence that should reset the ladder. The target holds no session (opening the review revoked them all), so their next sign-in is a full password + email code + second factor ceremony.

KEEP_DISABLED closes the review and leaves the account out of service.

reason.description: Written to the audit log, and required for BOTH decisions. Longer than the 280 the other actions allow, because this is the note an incident review actually reads — "why did we decide this was a fumbling admin rather than an attack" — and 280 characters is a tweet, not a rationale.

expectedVersion.description: The `reviewVersion` read from GET /admins/login-reviews. The update names it in its WHERE clause and refuses if it has moved. Without it, two super admins looking at the same queue can both act and the second silently overwrites the first — including in the direction that re-enables an account somebody had just decided to keep disabled. A stale value answers 400 validation_failed on `expectedVersion`; re-read the queue and retry.

retired.description: How many factors were actually retired. Reported because a reset on an account that had none is a different event from one that cleared two, and a UI that cannot tell them apart shows a success for a no-op.

reviewVersion.description: The version AFTER the write, so a client holding the list can update its row without re-fetching.

LoginReviewList.description: One page of the review queue. Carries COUNTS of distinct addresses and devices rather than the values themselves — a reviewer needs to know whether this was one actor or forty, and handing over the addresses would turn this into a way to read the authentication audit trail for any suspended account. No hashes of any kind appear here.

nextCursor.description: Pass back as `cursor` for the next page. Null on the last page. Opaque, and not a security boundary — everything in it is already in the body — so a malformed value starts from the beginning rather than erroring.

reviewVersion.description: Send this back as `expectedVersion` when resolving.

failureSummary.description: The evidence. `AdminCredential.failedAttempts` cannot answer any of this — it resets to zero on every lock — so without these counts a super admin is being asked to rule on an account with nothing but the fact that it was locked.

distinctIps.description: Distinct /24 (or /48) classes, not distinct addresses — a rotating residential IP inside one block is one actor, not sixty.

SessionStatus.description: Whether this browser is signed in, and as what. Five fields: role, permissions, authenticated, lastActiveAt, and message. It is what a frontend needs to decide what to render; `GET /auth/me` is where account details belong, and `Session` (returned at sign-in) is where the two deadlines are reported.

role.description: Re-read from the database, not taken from the access token's `rol` claim — a token lives fifteen minutes, so a demoted admin's claim is stale for that long, and this is the value a UI decides what to show from.

permissions.description: ALWAYS EMPTY for now. Permission calculation is not implemented. The field ships early so a client can be written against the final shape and will not need a contract change when it starts being populated — so do not infer permissions from its emptiness.

authenticated.description: Always `true`. NOT a discriminator: this route never answers `authenticated: false`. A dead session is a 401 whose `type` says why (`session_revoked`, `token_expired`, `unauthenticated`), and collapsing those into a 200 with a false flag would discard exactly the distinction a client needs.

lastActiveAt.description: When the backend last observed an eligible authenticated request on this session, as an ISO string. Null only when no session row was read.

SessionMessage.description: Why this authentication state exists. Code is the machine-readable contract; text is human-readable default wording.

code.description: Machine-readable status code describing why the session is in this state.

text.description: Default human-readable description. Informational only; clients must branch on `code`.

message.description: Switch on `code`; `text` is a default the panel may replace and must never be parsed.

KycPolicyUpsert.description: Every field is required, including the nullable ones. This write stores the whole row, so an omitted field would silently clear a value that is currently in force.

region.description: `*` for the global policy, or an ISO-3166-1 alpha-2 country. Uppercased.

level.description: The level this policy demands. `NONE` is a state an account can be in, never a level a policy can require.

required.description: Whether verification is owed generally in this region.

triggersOnly.description: When true, verification opens only once a configured trigger has fired. Refused if nothing is configured to trigger on — that combination would make verification permanently unreachable in the region.

renewalWorkflowId.description: Must be null unless renewal is enabled.

balanceThreshold.description: An exact decimal as a STRING, never a number: the column is `numeric(38,18)`, which carries more precision than a float64 mantissa holds. At most 20 integer and 18 decimal places, positive, no sign and no exponent.

lifetimeDepositThreshold.description: An exact decimal as a STRING, never a number: the column is `numeric(38,18)`, which carries more precision than a float64 mantissa holds. At most 20 integer and 18 decimal places, positive, no sign and no exponent.

lifetimeWithdrawalThreshold.description: An exact decimal as a STRING, never a number: the column is `numeric(38,18)`, which carries more precision than a float64 mantissa holds. At most 20 integer and 18 decimal places, positive, no sign and no exponent.

rollingWindowAmount.description: An exact decimal as a STRING, never a number: the column is `numeric(38,18)`, which carries more precision than a float64 mantissa holds. At most 20 integer and 18 decimal places, positive, no sign and no exponent.

thresholdCurrency.description: Required when any threshold is set, and must be null when none is. Uppercased.

features.description: Shape-validated only; the user backend checks the names against its own registry on read. Duplicates are rejected rather than collapsed.

subFeatures.description: A structured pair, not a joined string — storage joins them as `feature/subFeature`, so neither half may contain `/`.

reason.description: Required on every write. The version history is the compliance artifact, and a change with no stated reason is an audit finding waiting to happen.

expectedVersion.description: `0` to create. Otherwise the version you read.

KycPolicyDelete.description: Removes the policy so its region falls back to the global `*` rule. Not the same as disabling — a disabled country policy still takes precedence over the global one.

balanceThreshold.description: An exact decimal as a STRING, never a number: the column is `numeric(38,18)`, which carries more precision than a float64 mantissa holds. At most 20 integer and 18 decimal places, positive, no sign and no exponent.

lifetimeDepositThreshold.description: An exact decimal as a STRING, never a number: the column is `numeric(38,18)`, which carries more precision than a float64 mantissa holds. At most 20 integer and 18 decimal places, positive, no sign and no exponent.

lifetimeWithdrawalThreshold.description: An exact decimal as a STRING, never a number: the column is `numeric(38,18)`, which carries more precision than a float64 mantissa holds. At most 20 integer and 18 decimal places, positive, no sign and no exponent.

rollingWindowAmount.description: An exact decimal as a STRING, never a number: the column is `numeric(38,18)`, which carries more precision than a float64 mantissa holds. At most 20 integer and 18 decimal places, positive, no sign and no exponent.

version.description: Send this back as `expectedVersion` to edit this policy.

enforcementRejection.description: Null when the user backend will act on this policy. Otherwise the reason it would silently discard it — the policy is configured and enforcing nothing.

createVersion.description: What to send as `expectedVersion` to create a policy that does not exist yet.

versions.description: Newest first. A removal appears as a tombstone version with `enabled: false`.

items.description: As `KycPolicy`, but carrying `recordedAt` instead of `updatedAt` and no `enforcementRejection`.

effectiveLevel.description: The level this exemption is worth. It does not claim a provider verified anything.

reason.description: Required and non-empty. An exemption with no stated reason is an audit finding.

expiresAt.description: When the relief lapses; `null` is permanent. Required (but nullable) so permanence is always deliberate, and must be at least a minute in the future — a row that lands already expired grants nothing while still occupying the account’s only slot.

userId.description: Required alongside the id: the pair is what stops a stale row id being revoked against the wrong account.

live.description: Whether this exemption applies right now, evaluated by the database rather than by the admin service.

KycRenewalPayload.description:
The global KYC renewal configuration, and the whole of it. The same shape GET returns and POST accepts, so a screen reads, edits and writes back one object.

Both null means renewal is DISABLED: nothing expires because time passed, and no holder may redo a level early. That is a configuration rather than an absence — no default is ever substituted for a null.

There is deliberately no `renewalEnabled` field. It would be `mandatoryPeriodDays !== null` and nothing else, and a second copy of a fact the payload already carries eventually disagrees with the first.

mandatoryPeriodDays.description: X. How many days a completed verification stays valid. Null means verifications never expire.

voluntaryPeriodDays.description: Y. How many days before the holder may voluntarily redo a level that is still valid. Null keeps voluntary redo closed. Must be strictly less than mandatoryPeriodDays, and null when that is null.

KycHistoryAttempt.description: One KYC attempt, as the permanent record holds it. Sealed document numbers and names are absent from this shape and therefore unreachable from this surface.

level.description: From the persisted row. Never derived from provider metadata, vendor_data, the workflow name or a query parameter.

status.description: This service own state machine. IN_REVIEW is NON-TERMINAL — a human is deciding — and is never reinterpreted as EXPIRED merely because the hosted session window passed. The same row later shows APPROVED if the reviewer approves.

providerStatus.description: Didit word for it, verbatim and unnormalised.

workflowSource.description: Which configuration key supplied the workflow — how you tell an initial run from a renewal months later.

amlTotalHits.description: The hit COUNT. The hit list stays with the provider, whose lawful basis covers holding it.

documentType.description: Unsealed deliberately: it identifies nobody on its own, and a number without its type is ambiguous between a passport and a national id.

providerSessionExpiresAt.description: When the Didit hosted page stopped being completable. **NOT the KYC validity deadline for the account.** That is derived per level from the global renewal period and appears on the user-facing GET /kyc/status. Reading this as a validity deadline would suggest every verified user expires in a week.

createdAt.description: Microsecond-precision UTC — the value the keyset cursor compares.

isActiveCredential.description: Whether this attempt is the credential CURRENTLY in force for its level. False for every superseded success — which stays fully visible, because history is history.

KycHistoryDevice.description: A device the PROVIDER observed during the attempt. One session routinely produces two — a desktop hand-off to a phone for document capture.

deviceFingerprint.description: The PROVIDER fingerprint. Unrelated to this platform own session fingerprint; never compare them.

KycHistoryEvent.description: One inbound provider delivery, SUMMARISED. The verified webhook body is never included — it can carry a name, a date of birth and AML hit detail about third parties.

processingStatus.description: IGNORED is a success: a duplicate, or an event that would have walked a terminal status backwards.

signatureVariant.description: Which header authenticated the delivery — raw or canonical. The variant NAME, never a signature and never a secret.

Country.description: One country. `name` is display text; `isoCode` is the identifier. Both URLs are built from the object KEYS the row stores — they are null only when storage is unconfigured, never because an image is missing, since a country cannot be created without both.

imagesUpdatedAt.description: When the images were last replaced. Also the `?v=` value on both URLs.

Countries.description: Always an array, even when `isoCode` narrowed the query to one country — one shape for a caller to parse. Every entry carries the name AND the code beside both URLs, so the client never has to infer which country an image belongs to.

CountryCreateRequest.description:
A name, a code, and the two image KEYS the admin chose from the library or just uploaded.

**Keys, never URLs.** Validating a URL would mean deciding whether an attacker-supplied string points into our bucket — a game of prefix comparisons against redirects and unicode hostnames that is lost more often than won. A key is a path inside a bucket we name ourselves and cannot express another origin at all. Unknown properties are REJECTED, so sending `roundImageUrl` is a 400 naming the field rather than a silently ignored value.

Both images are required: a half-populated country is a broken render, and by this point the admin has already chosen both.

isoCode.description: ISO 3166-1 alpha-2. Trimmed and upper-cased, so `in` and `IN` are the same country.

roundImageKey.description: A `key` from GET /countries/images or POST /countries/images. Must be a **round** asset — the claimed slot is checked against the key's own, so a square asset offered here is refused rather than stored.

squareImageKey.description: As above, but must be a **square** asset.

CountryImageAsset.description: One image in the library. ASSET METADATA, not a country record — it deliberately carries no country name. An object in a bucket is not a country, and manufacturing a name from a key would invent a fact storage does not have.

key.description: The stable reference. Send this back to POST /countries.

type.description: Read from the key, never guessed from the file.

isoCode.description: The code the asset was FILED under. Metadata, not ownership — an asset uploaded for IN may legitimately be selected for another country.

CountryImages.description: The image library. NOT countries — see CountryImageAsset.
